name: ollam

attributes.attribute: held an oenach fair every three years at Samain
tenth ard ri in line from Éremón
credited with drawing up an early code of laws
credited with dividing the country into five parts

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The ollam was the highest rank among the seven levels of the Fili. The Fili was the Irish bardic order. The title also appears as ollamh and ollave. Someone at this rank had to recite all 250 chief tales. The bard also had to recite 100 of the lesser ones. The same word ollam appears in later legendary kingship. Ollam Fodla, also called Ollamh Fodhla, was a fabled king. He ruled at Tara. He is said to have set up the fair held every three years at Samain. Old Irish names this fair an oenach. He stood tenth in the line of ard ri. Ard ri means the high-kingship. The line was counted from Éremón. His renown rested on poetry and wisdom. He is also credited with drawing up an early code of laws. He shares the honor of dividing the country into five parts. Several other figures share that same credit. The bardic ollam and the legendary king Ollam Fodla thus share a single title across very different roles.

okr.objective: Define the ollam as the highest rank among the seven Fili grades and link the same title to the legendary king Ollam Fodla of Tara.
key_results: The ollam was the highest of the seven Fili grades in the bardic order.
An ollam recited all 250 chief tales of the country and 100 lesser tales.
The title also appears in the variant forms ollamh and ollave.
Ollam Fodla was a legendary king of Tara credited with founding a triennial oenach at Samain.
Ollam Fodla stood tenth in the ard ri line from Éremón and won renown for poetry and wisdom.
Ollam Fodla is also credited with drawing up an early code of laws and with the fivefold division of the country.
okr.evidence: MacKillop 2008, s.v. 'ollam'; Monaghan, Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore.
